intro: Hi! In this lesson you'll learn one small but very useful word: can. You'll use it to say what you can and can't do, to ask for help (Can you help me?) and to ask for permission (Can I come in?). Warm-up: can you swim?
teachingNotes: Can is the same for every subject and takes the base verb: no 'to' and no -s. Stress the node's common errors: *'I can to swim' → 'I can swim', *'She cans speak English' → 'She can speak English'.

Say why, plainly: can is a helper word. Helper words never take -s (she cooks, but she can cook: just remember it) and never need 'to' (like Indonesian 'bisa berenang', nothing goes between). Questions don't use do because can moves to the front by itself, like am/is/are. 'Base form' = the verb as in the dictionary: no -s, no -ing, no to. 'Can I have …?' = Boleh saya minta …? (have isn't 'punya' here).

Learners have just met do/does and over-use it: *'Do you can help me?' → 'Can you help me?', *'I don't can' → 'I can't'. With can, questions put can first and negatives use can't / cannot (one word). Short answers: Yes, I can. / No, I can't.

Indonesian uses three words where English uses one: bisa (ability), tolong / bisa tolong (request) and boleh (permission). 'Can you …?' as a request is not a question about ability, so the answer is Sure / Of course / Sorry, I can't. When someone asks 'Can I …?', the answer uses 'you': Yes, you can / Sorry, you can't (not 'Yes, I can').

Pronunciation: in positive sentences can is weak and short (sounds like 'kn'), while can't is stressed with a strong vowel (British /kɑːnt/, like a long 'kaant'; American /kænt/, close to 'kent' said with the mouth open wide) and the final t is often soft. Train learners to listen for the strong vowel, and to say can't clearly.
Limits: present only. Don't teach could for past ability, be able to, may or must yet. If a learner asks, say 'Could you …?' and 'May I …?' are a little more formal and come later.

keyPoints.title: can / can't for ability
keyPoints.explanation: Subject + can / can't + basic verb (no -s, no -ing, no to), the same for every subject. Normal verbs take -s with he/she (she cooks), but can is a helper word and never changes: she can cook. Questions: Can + subject + verb? (no do: can moves to the front by itself). Short answers: Yes, I can. / No, I can't.

examples.id: Sari bisa menyanyi dengan sangat bagus.
Nenek saya tidak bisa membaca bahasa Inggris.

examples.en: Can you cook? — Yes, I can.

keyPoints.title: Requests with Can you …?
keyPoints.explanation: Can you + verb (+ please)? asks someone to do something for you. Answer: Sure! / Of course. / Sorry, I can't.

examples.en: Can you pass the salt, please? — Sure!

keyPoints.title: Permission with Can I …?
keyPoints.explanation: Can I + verb? asks for permission. Give it with Yes, you can / Sure. Refuse with Sorry, you can't. Rules use the same words: You can't smoke here.

examples.en: Can I come in? — Yes, you can.

assessment.prompt: Make a question with can: you / speak / Javanese
acceptableAnswers: can you speak javanese
assessment.rubric: Correct: Can you speak Javanese? 'Do you can speak Javanese?' = 30. 'You can speak Javanese?' = 50. 'Can you to speak' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Make it negative: Rina can drive a car.
acceptableAnswers: rina can't drive a car
rina cannot drive a car
rina can not drive a car
she can't drive a car
she cannot drive a car
assessment.rubric: Correct: Rina can't / cannot drive a car. 'Rina doesn't can drive' = 30. 'Rina can't drives' = 50. 'Rina not can drive' = 30.

assessment.prompt: Listen. Can Dimas swim? Write yes or no.
assessment.listen: Dimas can't swim, but he can play football very well.
acceptableAnswers: no
no he can't
no he cannot
no he can not
assessment.rubric: Correct: No (he can't swim). 'Yes' = 0: the learner heard 'can' instead of the stressed 'can't'.

assessment.prompt: You are carrying three big boxes. Ask your colleague Budi to open the door for you. Start with 'Can you'.
acceptableAnswers: can you open the door
can you open the door please
can you please open the door
can you open the door for me
can you open the door for me please
budi can you open the door please
budi can you open the door
budi can you open the door for me please
assessment.rubric: Correct: Can you open the door (for me), please? Without please = 90. 'Do you can open' = 30. 'Can I open the door?' = 0 (that asks for permission).

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: Do you can turn on the AC, please?
acceptableAnswers: can you turn on the ac please
can you please turn on the ac
can you turn the ac on please
can you turn on the ac
can you turn the ac on
assessment.rubric: Correct: Can you turn on the AC, please? No 'do' with can. 'Do you turn on the AC?' = 30 (a different question). 'Can you to turn on' = 50.

assessment.prompt: You are in class and it's very hot. Ask your teacher for permission to open the window. Start with 'Can I'.
acceptableAnswers: can i open the window
can i open the window please
can i please open the window
excuse me can i open the window
excuse me can i open the window please
assessment.rubric: Correct: Can I open the window, please? Without please = 90. 'Can you open the window?' = 30 (a request, not permission). 'Do I can open' = 30.

assessment.prompt: A sign in front of a shop says NO PARKING. Complete: You ___ park here.
acceptableAnswers: can't
cannot
can not
mustn't
must not
assessment.rubric: Correct: can't / cannot (mustn't is also correct). 'can' = 0. 'don't can' = 30.

blocks.text: **Can** means *bisa*. Put it before a verb in its **base form** (the basic form, as in a dictionary: no -s, no -ing, no to): *I can swim. She can cook.* Can is the same for every subject: **no -s** with he/she/it (*she can*, not *she cans*) and **no to** after it (*I can swim*, not *I can to swim*).

id.text: **Can** artinya *bisa*. Letakkan sebelum kata kerja **bentuk dasar** (bentuk asli seperti di kamus: tanpa -s, tanpa -ing, tanpa to): *I can swim. She can cook.* Can sama untuk semua subjek: **tanpa -s** untuk he/she/it (*she can*, bukan *she cans*) dan **tanpa to** sesudahnya (*I can swim*, bukan *I can to swim*).

rows.id: Sari bisa menyanyi dengan sangat bagus. (*well* = dengan baik/bagus)
Adik laki-laki saya sudah bisa membaca. (*little brother* = adik laki-laki)

rows.en: We can speak Indonesian and English.
rows.id: Kami bisa berbahasa Indonesia dan Inggris.

blocks.text:
**Why no -s? You learned 'she cooks'.** Normal verbs (cook, work, play) get -s with he/she/it. **can** isn't a normal verb: it's a **helper word** that sits in front of another verb, and helper words **never change**. So: *she cooks*, but *she **can** cook*. Just remember it.
**Why no to?** It's like Indonesian: *bisa berenang*, with nothing in between. So **can swim**, with nothing in between.

id.text:
**Kenapa tanpa -s? Kamu sudah belajar 'she cooks'.** Kata kerja biasa (cook, work, play) diberi -s untuk he/she/it. **can** bukan kata kerja biasa: ia **kata bantu** yang berdiri di depan kata kerja lain, dan kata bantu **tidak pernah berubah**. Jadi: *she cooks*, tapi *she **can** cook*. Cukup dihafal.
**Kenapa tanpa to?** Sama seperti bahasa Indonesia: *bisa berenang*, tanpa kata di tengah. Jadi **can swim**, tanpa kata di tengah juga.

blocks.explain: Can is a helper word, and helper words never change: no -s for he/she, and no to before the verb. My mother can cook rendang.

id.explain: Can adalah kata bantu, dan kata bantu tidak pernah berubah: tanpa -s untuk he/she, dan tanpa to sebelum kata kerja. My mother can cook rendang.

blocks.text: Negative: **can't** (or **cannot**, written as one word) + base verb: *I can't dance.* Question: put **can** first: *Can you cook?* Short answers: **Yes, I can. / No, I can't.** Don't use do/does with can: *Can you cook?*, not *Do you can cook?* Why? **do/does** is only for verbs that have no helper. **can** is already a helper, so it moves to the front by itself, just like *am/is/are* (*Are you tired?*).

id.text: Kalimat negatif: **can't** (atau **cannot**, ditulis satu kata) + kata kerja dasar: *I can't dance.* Kalimat tanya: letakkan **can** di depan: *Can you cook?* Jawaban singkat: **Yes, I can. / No, I can't.** Jangan pakai do/does dengan can: *Can you cook?*, bukan *Do you can cook?* Kenapa? **do/does** hanya untuk kata kerja yang tidak punya kata bantu. **can** sudah kata bantu, jadi ia sendiri yang pindah ke depan, sama seperti *am/is/are* (*Are you tired?*).

rows.id: Nenek saya tidak bisa membaca bahasa Inggris.

rows.en: I can't dance, but I can sing.
rows.id: Saya tidak bisa menari, tapi saya bisa menyanyi.

rows.en: Can you cook? — Yes, I can.
Can Budi play the guitar? — No, he can't.
rows.id: Budi bisa main gitar? — Tidak, dia tidak bisa.

blocks.text: Listen carefully! In a sentence, **can** is short and quiet, almost 'kn': *I can swim.* **Can't** is long and strong, and the **t** is often very soft. British English says it like a long 'kaant'; American English sounds close to 'kent' with the mouth open wide. So listen for the strong vowel: short and quiet = **can**, long and strong = **can't**.

id.text: Dengarkan baik-baik! Dalam kalimat, **can** pendek dan pelan, hampir seperti 'kn': *I can swim.* **Can't** panjang dan tegas, dan bunyi **t**-nya sering sangat pelan. Bahasa Inggris British mengucapkannya seperti 'kaant' yang panjang; bahasa Inggris Amerika terdengar mirip 'kent' dengan mulut terbuka lebar. Jadi dengarkan vokalnya: pendek dan pelan = **can**, panjang dan tegas = **can't**.

blocks.explain: Answer with the same helper word as the question: Can …? → Yes, she can. Helper words never take -s, so not 'she cans'.

id.explain: Jawab dengan kata bantu yang sama seperti di pertanyaan: Can …? → Yes, she can. Kata bantu tidak pernah diberi -s, jadi bukan 'she cans'.

blocks.text: **Can you** + verb … ? is a polite way to ask someone to do something, like *tolong* or *bisa tolong …?* Add **please** to sound friendly. It's a request, not a question about ability, so the answer is **Sure! / Of course. / Sorry, I can't.**

id.text: **Can you** + kata kerja … ? adalah cara sopan untuk meminta orang melakukan sesuatu, seperti *tolong* atau *bisa tolong …?* Tambahkan **please** supaya terdengar ramah. Ini permintaan, bukan pertanyaan tentang kemampuan, jadi jawabannya **Sure! / Of course. / Sorry, I can't.**

rows.en: Can you pass the salt, please? — Sure!
Can you call me later? — Of course.
Can you wait five minutes? — Sorry, I can't. I'm late.
rows.id: Bisa tunggu lima menit? — Maaf, nggak bisa. Saya sudah terlambat.

blocks.text: Not *Do you can help me?* There is no do with can: **Can you help me?** And a request without please (*Help me!*) can sound rude in English, even though *Bantu saya!* sounds normal in Indonesian.

id.text: Bukan *Do you can help me?* Tidak ada do kalau memakai can: **Can you help me?** Dan permintaan tanpa please (*Help me!*) bisa terdengar kasar dalam bahasa Inggris, walaupun *Bantu saya!* terdengar biasa dalam bahasa Indonesia.

blocks.prompt: Your friend asks: 'Can you close the window, please?' You want to help. What do you say?
blocks.explain: It's a request, not a question about what you're able to do, so just agree: Sure! (or Of course.) 'Yes, I do' answers a do-question.

id.explain: Ini permintaan, bukan pertanyaan tentang kemampuanmu, jadi cukup setuju: Sure! (atau Of course.) 'Yes, I do' adalah jawaban untuk pertanyaan dengan do.

blocks.text: **Can I** + verb … ? asks for permission, like *boleh saya …?* To say yes: **Yes, you can. / Sure. / Of course.** To say no: **Sorry, you can't.** Rules and signs use the same words: *You can sit anywhere. You can't smoke here.*

id.text: **Can I** + kata kerja … ? dipakai untuk minta izin, seperti *boleh saya …?* Untuk bilang ya: **Yes, you can. / Sure. / Of course.** Untuk bilang tidak: **Sorry, you can't.** Aturan dan tanda juga memakai kata yang sama: *You can sit anywhere. You can't smoke here.*

rows.en: Can I come in? — Yes, you can.

rows.id: Boleh saya duduk di sini? — Silakan.

rows.en: Can I take a photo? — Sorry, you can't.
rows.id: Boleh saya ambil foto? — Maaf, tidak boleh.
Kamu boleh duduk di mana saja.

blocks.text: Answer with **you**: *Can I come in? — Yes, **you** can.* Not *Yes, I can*: that talks about you, not the person who asks. In Indonesian the answer is just *boleh*, with no person, but English needs **you**.

id.text: Jawab dengan **you**: *Can I come in? — Yes, **you** can.* Bukan *Yes, I can*: itu membicarakan dirimu sendiri, bukan orang yang bertanya. Dalam bahasa Indonesia jawabannya cukup *boleh*, tanpa orang, tapi bahasa Inggris butuh **you**.

blocks.prompt: You are at a friend's house and you are thirsty. Which question asks for permission?
options: Can I have a glass of water?
Can you have a glass of water?
Do I can have a glass of water?
blocks.explain: Permission for yourself = Can I …? Here Can I have …? means 'Boleh saya minta …?' (have isn't 'punya' here). 'Can you have …' is about your friend, and there is no do with can.

id.explain: Izin untuk dirimu sendiri = Can I …? Di sini Can I have …? artinya 'Boleh saya minta …?' (have di sini bukan 'punya'). 'Can you have …' membicarakan temanmu, dan tidak ada do kalau memakai can.

suggestedQuestions: How can I hear the difference between can and can't?
Why is it wrong to say 'Do you can help me?'
Is 'Can I …?' polite enough with my boss?
What's the difference between can and may?

id.intro: Hai! Di pelajaran ini kamu belajar satu kata kecil yang sangat berguna: can. Kamu akan memakainya untuk mengatakan apa yang bisa dan tidak bisa kamu lakukan, untuk minta tolong (Can you help me?) dan untuk minta izin (Can I come in?). Pemanasan: can you swim?

Kenapa 'Do you can help me?' salah?
Apakah 'Can I …?' cukup sopan untuk bicara dengan atasan?
